opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I get a lot, and I think the distinction matters.

PagedAttention is an idea. It's a research contribution from the 2023 paper, which observed that KV cache memory during LLM serving was being wasted badly, through fragmentation and over-reservation, and borrowed the operating-system concept of virtual memory and paging to manage it. Splitting the KV cache into fixed-size blocks that don't need to be contiguous dramatically improved memory utilization, which let you batch many more requests and get much higher throughput. That was a clean, important insight, and it's why the project took off.

vLLM is something else now. It started as the reference implementation of that paper, but if you look at the codebase today, PagedAttention is a small fraction of it. vLLM has become a general-purpose inference engine. It has continuous batching, prefix caching, chunked prefill, speculative decoding, quantization, many kinds of parallelism — tensor, pipeline, expert, data — and disaggregated prefill and decode. It supports hundreds of model architectures and many hardware backends: NVIDIA, AMD, TPUs, Intel, and various accelerators from other vendors. Much of the hard work is in that integration layer, making all of these features compose correctly and run efficiently together.

I'd put it this way: the paper answered one research question, how to manage memory for attention efficiently. vLLM tries to answer an engineering and ecosystem question: how do you give everyone, whether model developers, hardware vendors, or companies deploying models, one open, fast, reliable layer for running large models? That's more about software architecture, community, and sustained maintenance than about any single algorithm.

There's a cultural difference too. A paper is finished once it's published. A system like vLLM is never finished. New models come out every week, with new attention variants, new MoE designs, new hardware, and the system has to keep absorbing them. Much of my own work, especially on things like the torch.compile integration and the hardware plugin system, has been about making vLLM extensible enough to keep up with that, rather than optimizing one kernel.

So PagedAttention is where vLLM came from, but it's no longer what vLLM is. It's become infrastructure.

r001.rationale: It says PagedAttention borrowed operating-system virtual memory and paging to manage the KV cache during LLM serving.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes PagedAttention as a memory-management idea from vLLM as a general-purpose inference engine and infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It describes vLLM needing to absorb new model designs and hardware, and to integrate them so features run efficiently together.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, because people often conflate the two, and I think the distinction matters a lot for understanding what vLLM is today.

PagedAttention is an algorithm. It's a specific idea: treat the KV cache the way an operating system treats virtual memory, break it into fixed-size blocks, keep a block table that maps logical positions to physical blocks, and let the attention kernel read from non-contiguous memory. That single idea solves a very concrete problem, which is that the old way of pre-allocating contiguous memory for each request's maximum possible length wasted something like 60 to 80 percent of GPU memory. Fix that, and you can batch many more requests at once, and throughput goes up dramatically. The paper came out of Berkeley in 2023, and vLLM was essentially the artifact built to demonstrate it.

But vLLM the project is a system, and systems are much bigger than any one algorithm. If you look at what people are actually running in production now, PagedAttention is one component among many, and honestly it's not even the component that most of the engineering effort goes into anymore. There's continuous batching, which is a scheduler-level idea that originally came from Orca, not from the PagedAttention paper at all. There's prefix caching, speculative decoding, chunked prefill, quantization support across many formats, tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism, multi-LoRA serving, structured output and guided decoding, and the whole model zoo, which means supporting hundreds of architectures, including multimodal models, with all their little quirks. Plus the hardware side: NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, TPU, various accelerators from Chinese vendors, CPU. Each of those is a serious amount of work that has nothing to do with paging memory.

And there's a subtle point here. In the beginning, the attention kernel itself was PagedAttention, meaning vLLM had its own custom CUDA kernel that understood block tables. Today, a lot of the kernels vLLM runs are FlashAttention, FlashInfer, and others, which have all adopted the paged memory layout as a standard interface. So the idea from the paper won, in the sense that it became the common convention across the entire ecosystem. But vLLM no longer owns that kernel exclusively, and it doesn't need to. The idea got absorbed into the infrastructure.

So the way I'd put it: the paper is the seed, and the system is the tree. The paper answered one question very well, how to manage KV cache memory. The system has to answer the question that users actually ask, which is, how do I run this model on this hardware with this latency and this cost, reliably, every day. That second question never has a single answer, which is why vLLM is a continuously evolving open-source project with hundreds of contributors rather than a finished research artifact.

I'd actually say that if you still think of vLLM as "the PagedAttention implementation," you're missing most of what the community has built over the last few years. The research origin gave it credibility and a great starting point, but what keeps it alive is the systems work and the community around it.

r001.rationale: It describes PagedAttention as managing the KV cache like virtual memory: dividing it into fixed-size blocks, mapping logical positions to physical blocks, and allowing non-contiguous access.

r002.rationale: It contrasts PagedAttention as one KV-cache algorithm with vLLM as a broader inference system incorporating scheduling, decoding, model support, and hardware support.

r003.rationale: It says vLLM must support many model architectures and hardware platforms, and frames users’ needs as running a particular model on particular hardware with suitable latency and cost.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish them by scope. PagedAttention is a technique for managing the KV cache during inference. Instead of reserving one large, contiguous chunk of memory for each request, it organizes the cache into blocks. That reduces wasted memory and lets you serve more requests concurrently.

vLLM is the inference system around that idea. It has to handle scheduling, execute models efficiently, support different model architectures and hardware, and provide a serving interface. PagedAttention is an important foundation, but it isn’t the whole system.

So the paper explains a key idea and demonstrates its benefits. The ongoing work on vLLM is making all the pieces work together as a practical, reliable inference engine.

r001.rationale: It describes block-based KV-cache management, but does not connect the technique to operating-system virtual-memory ideas.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes PagedAttention as a KV-cache technique from vLLM as the broader inference system handling scheduling, execution, architecture and hardware support, and serving.

r003.rationale: It mentions supporting different model architectures and hardware, but does not identify the coupling between models and hardware as a challenge vLLM must accommodate.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish the core technique from the system built around it. PagedAttention addresses a specific problem: how to manage the KV cache efficiently during inference. Instead of requiring a large, contiguous allocation for each request, it organizes the cache into blocks, which reduces wasted memory and makes sharing possible.

vLLM is the inference system that uses that technique. It also has to schedule requests, batch work, execute the model efficiently, and provide a serving interface. Those pieces have to work together to deliver good throughput and latency.

So PagedAttention was the starting point, but vLLM has a broader scope. You can use PagedAttention in another system, and vLLM’s development involves many improvements beyond PagedAttention itself.

r001.rationale: It describes block-based KV-cache management, but does not connect it to operating-system virtual-memory ideas.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes PagedAttention as a KV-cache technique from vLLM as a broader inference and serving system.

r003.rationale: It mentions efficient model execution but does not identify accommodating model–hardware coupling as a challenge.
